source_document.body:
2026 Paris Motor Show • The Volkswagen Group's Affordable BEV Quartet Has Almost Reached 150,000 Orders
Based on Tesla's Latest Decision, the Cybertruck Is on Its Way Out; Will There Be a Replacement?
6 photos
Photo: Tesla
Tesla is cutting the losses of its failed Cybertruck program by scrapping plans to offer a right-hand-drive variant of the electric pickup. Reservation holders in Australia and New Zealand, some of them with seven-year-old deposits, have been notified of the cancellation and will receive their money back. This is a step that Tesla also took in 2023 for the refreshed Model S and Model X, which were canceled three years later.
The Cybertruck was probably Elon Musk's most beloved car project, until the Roadster, that is. Tesla's CEO spent countless sleepless nights imagining impossible features for the electric pickup truck. Not only did the Cybertruck have to be the toughest EV on earth, but Musk wanted it to be bulletproof and at the same time float like a boat. A real apocalypse vehicle , as he and, by extension, his fans, proclaimed.
Musk was so excited about the Cybertruck that he genuinely thought a 250,000 annual production would still not be enough. After the 2019 unveiling, reservations piled up and quickly surpassed the one-million mark. Everyone thought that the Cybertruck would replace the Ford F-150 as the best-selling truck in America.
And yet, when it started shipping at the end of 2023, it disappointed almost everyone. Reservation holders canceled their orders, and actual deliveries dried up in less than a year after the start of production. Since 2024, Tesla could barely sell 30,000 Cybertrucks in a year, and that's counting the trucks that Musk bought for his companies, including SpaceX.
Saving the Cybertruck proved harder than anticipated The first move Tesla tried to improve Cybertrucks' lackluster sales was to expand the Cybertruck addressable market. It did so by starting sales in Mexico, followed by the Middle East and Asia. Tesla currently sells the Cybertruck in South Korea, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Jordan, and Israel, in addition to the US, Canada, and Mexico.
Photo: Tesla As this didn't meaningfully revive Cybertruck sales, Tesla tried removing some features to lower the price. The Cybertruck RWD proved an utter failure, as Tesla offered a modest discount while removing Cybertruck's most appealing features. After this strategy failed, Tesla went in the opposite direction with the Cybertruck AWD Standard. Sold at $59,990 while retaining most beloved features, the Cybertruck AWD looked like a winner.
However, it didn't take long before Tesla raised the price to $69,990, just 10 days later. In August, it hiked the price again to $74,990. Many Tesla fans were convinced that the demand was off the charts, hence the price increase. Sadly, it was just a move to cut losses, as Cybertruck sales numbers would soon prove. Indeed, with so many new cutting-edge technologies under the hood and low sales numbers, the Cybertruck program was bleeding money.
This became obvious when Tesla reported the second and third quarter delivery numbers. Instead of tens of thousands of units delivered (the Cybertruck line has a theoretical capacity of 125,000 units per year), Tesla reported only 8,295 "Other Models" delivered in Q3 2026. This category also includes the Cybercab and Semi. The numbers show the Cybertruck is on track to become the biggest new car failure in automotive history.
Right-hand-drive Cybertruck is out, what happens next? Tesla is obviously aware of that, and this is why it no longer wants to build a right-hand-drive model. While no official announcement was made, reservation holders in Australia and New Zealand were recently notified in an email that their reservations have been canceled . "After careful consideration, plans to produce Cybertruck for Australia and New Zealand have been discontinued," the email wrote. "As a result, we’re unable to fulfil your reservation and it will be cancelled."
The move doesn't come as a complete surprise, after Tesla had already closed the Australian reservation page in 2022. The carmaker didn't refund the reservation holders until now, though. This means that some have been hoping to eventually get a Cybertruck, even though seven years have passed. However, Tesla never produced an RHD variant of the Cybertruck, and never will. If anything, it might scrap the Cybertruck altogether.
Photo: Tesla While building an RHD variant of an already slow-selling model didn't make sense, everyone is wondering how long the Cybertruck can survive. The electric pickup truck pioneered some cutting-edge technologies. Still, its polarizing design and underwhelming specifications made it a tough sell. Will Tesla turn it into something else, possibly a full-size SUV, as many asked? Or will it kill it altogether, as others expect?
Tesla has already walked down this path with the Model S and Model X Considering the low Cybertruck sales, Tesla's decision is entirely justified. The Cybertruck swallowed tons of money, and repeated changes in the truck's design and engineering only deepened the loss. Building a right-hand-drive variant in even lower numbers would've written off more money, especially as Australia and New Zealand were its only markets. Even adding the UK wouldn't have changed much, as the Model S and Model X showed.
The two veteran models had a much larger customer base, with the RHD variant sold in Japan, the UK, and other countries. And yet, Tesla refused to build a new RHD variant when it refreshed the Model S and Model X in 2021. It tried to sell the LHD variant in the RHD markets, with little success. Three years after admitting that the RHD variants don't make sense , Tesla retired the Model S and Model X in all markets.
Scrapping the RHD Cybertruck is not much different from what Tesla did in 2023 when it canceled the RHD Model S and Model X. The two OG Tesla EVs survived for only three years after that decision. I'm not sure that the Cybertruck has that much left, considering that it sells far worse than the Model S and Model X did.
